claims.event: Yan Gaoqing, styled Xin, acting prefect of Changshan, killed Li Qincou and rose against An Lushan; when Changshan fell he cursed Lushan and was dismembered on the Tianjin Bridge at sixty-five.
Elder brother of Yan Gaoqing who earned top marks in the document examination.
Pinglu deputy commissioner ordered to seize Youzhou, executed by An Lushan when the plot leaked.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Listed among the biographies of Loyalty and Righteousness.
Kinsman of Yan Gaoqing who in Pingyuan trained loyal men, beheaded Duan Ziguang and sent his nephew Lu Ti to Changshan.
Vice minister of personnel who praised the Yan brothers.
Rebel who recommended Yan Gaoqing, then after his rising had him dismembered at Luoyang.
Chief administrator of Changshan who killed Li Qincou with Yan Gaoqing and spat blood at his captors before being hacked apart.
Foster son of An Lushan, lured and beheaded at Changshan.
Zhending magistrate who plotted against the rebels and became military aide.
Neiqiu magistrate who joined the plot and carried Qincou’s head to the capital.
Son of Yan Gaoqing who carried plans and escorted the captives to the capital.
Taiyuan intendant who stole the credit for the captives and refused to relieve Changshan.
Placed in command of Youzhou by An Lushan.
Placed in command of Youzhou by An Lushan.
Recluse summoned by Yan Gaoqing to plan strategy.
Recluse who led a hundred horsemen raising dust as vanguard.
Killed by the rebels, his head paraded through the commanderies.
Rebel envoy beheaded by Yan Zhenqing.
Nephew of Yan Zhenqing sent to Changshan, killed with Jiming.
Assistant who seized Gao Miao and He Qiannian.
Local leader who helped kill Li Qincou and carried his head to the capital.
Officer of Li Qincou killed at Changshan.
Rebel general seized at Mancheng.
City commandant who lured Gao Miao with wine.
Rebel general captured by Feng Qian.
Warrior who refused Wang Chengye’s order to waylay the prisoners.
Tang ruler who promoted Wang Chengye.
Rebel who fled from Raoyang.
Led Pinglu troops against Changshan.
Rebel general who joined the attack on Changshan.
Younger son of Yan Gaoqing killed for his father’s refusal to surrender.

label.en: Minister of the Court for the Imperial Insignia

claims.event: Slandered after death by Zhang Tongyou, later posthumously Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent with the title Loyal and Upright, then Minister of Education; buried by Quanming at Fengqi Plain.
Slandered Yan Gaoqing to Yang Guozhong and as prefect of Pu’an was beaten to death on the retired ruler’s order.
Minister to whom Zhang Tongyou slandered Yan Gaoqing.
Tang ruler at Fengxiang who received Yan Zhenqing’s memorial and appointed Quanming magistrate of Pi.
Memorialized on Gaoqing’s behalf, as prefect of Pu sent Quanming to find kin, and arranged Chunqing’s sons’ marriages.
Retook Changshan with Guo Ziyi and freed the Yan and Yuan households; later besieged by Shi Siming.
Retook Changshan with Li Guangbi.
His relatives were freed from prison; buried in the same grave as Gaoqing and later escorted home by Quanming.
Wife of Yan Gaoqing, enfeoffed as Lady of Qinghe.
Granted a posthumous fifth-rank office and buried with Jiming.
Granted a posthumous fifth-rank office and buried with Lu Ti.
Recovered a lock of Gaoqing’s hair and presented it to the retired ruler.
Buried his father and Lüqian, captured by Shi Siming and escaped, ransomed kin, supported over three hundred dependents, magistrate of Pi and military aide of Pengzhou.
Sent Quanming back before Changshan fell.
Besieged Li Guangbi, captured Quanming, and later submitted to the court.
Passed the Mingjing and Baodi examinations at sixteen, recalled a thousand convicts from memory, saved Wei Zheng’s descendant, died assistant magistrate of Yanshi entrusting his sons to Zhenqing.
Chief administrator who released Chunqing and as minister of rites praised Jia Xun.
Ancestor of Zhan, whom Chunqing saved.
Princess to whom Chunqing appealed for Zhan’s life.
Nephew of Yan Gaoqing, sheriff of Boye, who died with him and was posthumously Director of the Court of Judicial Review.
Jia Xun of Huayuan defeated the Tibetans, bridged the Luan River, served as An Lushan’s deputy and prefect of Boling, agreed to Gaoqing’s plot and was hanged; posthumously Grand Preceptor.
Led the northern campaign across the Luan River.
Military governor of Fanyang who recommended Jia Xun.
Took Jia Xun as deputy, then rebelled and posted him to Youzhou.
Posthumously honored Jia Xun’s father as prefect of Changshan.
Betrayed Jia Xun’s conspiracy.

label.en: Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent
Director of the Court of Judicial Review
Agricultural Colony Commissioner of the Jingsai Army
Deputy Grand Protector of the Eastern Pacification

claims.event: Nephew of Jia Xun, military commissioner at Yongping who guarded Dezong’s traveling court during Zhu Ci’s revolt and bluntly admonished him.
Rebel whose revolt drove Dezong from the capital and who later fled.
Tang ruler impressed by Yin Lin who took no offense at his admonition.
Named by Yin Lin as his father’s cousin and former deputy military governor of Fanyang.
Fought beside Yin Lin under the rebel siege.
Zhang Xun of Nanyang, magistrate of Qinghe and Zhenyuan, executed Hua Nanjin, rose against An Lushan, and held Yongqiu for months against Linghu Chao.
Elder brother of Zhang Xun, investigating censor.
Dominated the court; Zhang Xun refused to seek his favor.
Tyrannical chief clerk of Zhenyuan executed by Zhang Xun.
Rebel against whom Zhang Xun took up arms.
Rebel leader who seized Songzhou and was killed at Xiangyi by Lu Yin.
Governor of Qiao who surrendered and forced Zhang Xun to serve him.
Prince of Wu and governor of Lingchang who assembled Henan forces, appointed Jia Ben censor and entrusted Zhang Xun with the east.
District captain of Danfu who attacked Songzhou, joined Zhang Xun at Yongqiu and was trampled to death.
Magistrate of Dunqiu who killed Zhang Tongwu.
Magistrate of Yongqiu who joined the rebels and besieged Zhang Xun repeatedly.
Rebel general who attacked Yongqiu with Linghu Chao.
Prince of Guo and military governor of Henan who made Zhang Xun his vanguard.

label.en: Left Vice Minister of the Department of State Affairs

claims.event: Held Ningling and Suiyang with Xu Yuan against Yin Ziqi, devised ruses, killed his concubine to feed his starving men, and sent Nan Jiyun for relief.
Prince of Guo who fell back to Linhuai, stinted rewards, sent half of Suiyang’s grain away, and was replaced by Helan Jinming.
Governor of Jiyin who surrendered his command to the rebels.
Rebel general who tried to cut Zhang Xun’s supply lines and joined the Suiyang assault.
Prefect of Suiyang who served under Zhang Xun, managed supplies, and killed his servants to feed the troops.
Magistrate of Chengfu who joined Zhang Xun at Suiyang and was made a bureau director of personnel.
Officer sent by Zhang Xun to fight north of Ningling.
Fought at Ningling, shot Yin Ziqi in the eye, cut off a finger before Helan Jinming, and fought back into Suiyang.
Rebel leader whose death preceded the Suiyang assault.
Son of An Lushan who sent Yin Ziqi against Suiyang.
Rebel commander besieging Suiyang, shot in the left eye by Nan Jiyun.
Xu Yuan’s officer who defected and was beheaded by Zhang Xun.
Senior general secretly in contact with the enemy.
Rebel officer persuaded by Zhang Xun to surrender with his followers.
Censor-in-Chief and military governor at Linhuai who refused to relieve Suiyang.
Held Pengcheng under Helan Jinming and refused Nan Jiyun’s plea.
Held Pengcheng and refused to relieve Suiyang.
Posted Xu Shuji to check Helan Jinming.
Gave Nan Jiyun a hundred horses at Zhenyuan.
City magistrate at Ningling whose three thousand men joined Nan Jiyun.

label.en: Bureau Director of the Ministry of Personnel

claims.event: Captured when Suiyang fell, refused to submit to Yin Ziqi and was killed at forty-nine; posthumously grand commander-in-chief of Yangzhou, his portrait placed in the Lingyan Pavilion.

Captured with Zhang Xun, sent toward Luoyang and killed at Yanshi; great-grandson of Xu Jingzong, earlier demoted by Zhangqiu Jianqiong, prefect of Suiyang; posthumously grand commander-in-chief of Jingzhou.
Took Suiyang, pried open Zhang Xun’s mouth and had him killed.
Called Nan Eight by Zhang Xun, refused to submit and was killed; posthumously given honors equal to the Three Excellencies and grand commander-in-chief of Yangzhou.
Killed with Zhang Xun; posthumously grand commander-in-chief of Luzhou.
Killed with Zhang Xun at Suiyang.
Rebel leader to whom Yin Ziqi planned to send Xu Yuan.
Prince who fled to Linhuai despite Zhang Xun’s sister’s plea.
Elder sister of Zhang Xun married into the Lu family, who sewed for the army and was killed before him.
Rebel general fought by Zhang Xun.
Tang ruler who sent Zhang Hao to relieve Suiyang.
Vice director of the Secretariat who replaced Helan Jinming in Henan, arrived three days late, and commissioned Zhang Xun’s eulogy.
Replaced by Zhang Hao as military governor of Henan.
Military governor of Zhedong in the Suiyang relief.
Military governor of Zhexi in the Suiyang relief.
Military governor of Huainan in the Suiyang relief.
Military governor of Qingzhou in the Suiyang relief.
Drafting officer who wrote Zhang Xun’s eulogy.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Defended Zhang Xun’s record.
Celebrated scholar whose defense of Zhang Xun ended the debate.
Ranked Zhang Xun, Xu Yuan and Nan Jiyun among the most distinguished since Zhide.
Ranked in the highest tier by Dezong.
Ranked in the highest tier by Dezong.
Ranked in the highest tier by Dezong.
Son of Zhang Xun restored to office in the Zhenyuan reign.
Tang ruler down to whose reign descendants of the loyal ministers were sought.
Right Chancellor and great-grandfather of Xu Yuan.
Recruited Xu Yuan to Jiannan and had him demoted when he refused marriage to his daughter.
Rebel whose rising led to Xu Yuan’s appointment.
Tang ruler who appointed Xu Yuan prefect of Suiyang.

label.en: Unequalled Opening of the Office with Ceremonial Equal to the Three Excellencies

claims.event: Killed at Suiyang cursing Xu Yuan according to his son Quji; welcomed Nan Jiyun and Lei Wanchun; praised by the historian as a man of fierce honor.
Son of Zhang Xun who in the Dali reign memorialized to strip Xu Yuan of honors; the court rejected the charge.
Accused by Quji of disloyalty when Suiyang fell; defended by the court and by Han Yu.
Had Zhang Xun and his officers flayed while sparing Xu Yuan.
Deliberated with Quji and the court over Xu Yuan’s record.
Read Li Han’s biography of Zhang Xun and defended Xu Yuan in writing.
Author of a biography of Zhang Xun that omitted Xu Yuan.
Nan Jiyun of Dunqiu, once a boatman, served Zhang Zhao and Shang Heng, then joined Zhang Xun and volunteered for the deadliest tasks; a peerless archer.
Rebel against whom Zhang Zhao raised troops.
Assistant magistrate of Juye who raised troops and made Nan Jiyun a commander.
Fought Li Tingwang with Nan Jiyun as vanguard and tried to recall him with gold and silk.
Rebel at Bianzhou fought by Shang Heng.
Rebel whose rising led to the demotion of Nan Jiyun’s son.
Lieutenant general of Zhang Xun who stood unmoving with six bolts in his face at Yongqiu.
Besieged Yongqiu, was astonished by Lei Wanchun, and was routed by Zhang Xun.
Grandnephew of Yao Chong, assistant magistrate of Shou’an and magistrate of Chengfu, who defended Suiyang and rose to prefect of Dongping.
Kaiyuan chancellor, great-uncle of Yao Yin.
Father of Yao Yin, prefect of Chuzhou.
